topic.title: Why Everyone Stopped Buying Crocs (and Then Didn't)

title: Why Everyone Stopped Buying Crocs (and Then Didn't)
description:
Crocs took in $847.4M in a single year. A year later it lost $185.1M, cut its staff and warned in its own annual report that it might not survive. Then the same ugly shoe came back bigger than ever.
This is the whole rise, fall and comeback, told from Crocs' own SEC filings: the Canadian foam, the craze, the discounting that broke it, the flat years, the charms and collaborations that turned the clog into a canvas, and the second big bet.

Chapters
0:00 The arc
0:52 One shoe
2:44 The craze
4:55 The crack
6:32 The crash
8:36 The flat years
9:51 The canvas
11:59 The second bet
13:50 What happened

A documentary built from public filings, reporting and licensed photos.
Based on public records and reporting. Not financial or legal advice.

lines.text: Crocs. The foam clog half the world called ugly.
At the height of the craze, the company sold $847.4M in a single year.
It shipped 46.9M pairs of them.
A year later, sales had fallen, and Crocs lost $185.1M.
Its share price went from $75.21 to $0.79.
And its own annual report warned it might not survive.
Everyone knew how this story ended. Fads die.
Except this one came back. Last year the company sold $4.04B.
Nothing about it had changed. The holes, the foam, the shape were all the same.
So what sank Crocs, and what brought it back? It wasn't a rival, and it wasn't a better shoe.
It was what the company did with the shoe it already had. Twice. Once wrong, and once right.
This is how a shoe everyone stopped buying became a business selling $4.04B a year.
Chapter one. One shoe, and the Canadian foam it was made from.
So where did this shoe come from? The company's early filings give its home as Niwot, a small town in Colorado, outside Boulder.
But the shoe itself wasn't American. It was made by a Canadian company, Foam Creations, in Quebec City.
Crocs modified that shoe, and in 2002 it began selling it in the United States.
It was meant for boaters and water sports. It was light, it gripped a wet deck, and it didn't leave marks.
There was one model, the Beach, in 6 colours.
A size large weighed about 6 ounces, far lighter than most shoes.
So what made it different? The foam. Crocs called it croslite, a closed-cell resin, soft and light and resistant to odour.
In 2004, Crocs bought Foam Creations, its factory and the formula.
Until late 2004, every pair came out of that one factory in Quebec City.
Foam Creations hadn't only made shoes. With the same foam it made spa pillows, seats for kayaks and canoes, and scuba diving fins.
It never patented that formula. It kept it as a trade secret.
Could a rival just copy it? Plenty tried, almost at once. In Canada, Crocs sued a rival called Holey Soles, saying its clog was identical to the Beach in every material respect.
And even then, the Quebec factory made only about 16.8% of the company's shoes. The rest came from a plant Crocs bought in Mexico, and from outside makers in China, Florida and Italy.
In the United States, it went further. Armed with fresh patents on the shoe, it asked the International Trade Commission to ban imports of the copies.
So did anyone actually buy it? In its first full year of selling, Crocs took in $1.2M.
Then $108.6M. 6M pairs in a year.
And one shoe carried the company. The Beach model brought in about 60.9% of all its footwear sales.
A pair cost $19.99 to $59.99.
A shoe for boats was about to become a shoe for everyone. And that's where the trouble started.
Chapter two. The craze, and a company that tried to ride it for ever.
What do you do when everyone suddenly wants your shoe? You raise money. In February 2006, Crocs sold its shares to the public on Nasdaq.
The company raised about $96.9M for itself from the sale.
It used the money to pay its debts, build more factory capacity and push into new countries.
Crocs sold through shops, its own website, and a new trick: small company kiosks in shopping malls, a cart in the corridor with a wall of colours.
That year, sales jumped to $354.7M.
The clog left the dock, for hospital corridors and restaurant kitchens.
Crocs even made a line for them, Crocs at Work, for healthcare and food workers.
And a medical line, Crocs Rx, sold as relief for sore feet: heel pain, diabetes, the days after surgery.
And not only workers. Crocs made them for men, for women and for children, in more colours every season.
By early the next year, Crocs were sold in more than 11,000 store locations in the United States, in more than 80 countries, and in more than 25 models.
And what do you sell to people who already own the shoe? That December, Crocs found an answer. It bought a small company called Jibbitz for $13.5M.
Jibbitz made little charms that snapped into the holes of the shoe.
By the end of the year, there were more than 900 designs.
The next year, Jibbitz alone sold $67.5M. Remember that charm. It matters later.
And it went shopping. A hockey and lacrosse gear maker called Fury. An Italian design studio, EXO, in Padova. A sandal maker, Ocean Minded. Another footwear brand, Bite.
Its annual report set out the plan: grow far beyond the shoe, into whole new categories.
And the shoes? 21.6M pairs one year. 46.9M pairs the next.
Sales hit $847.4M.
And in the last months of the year, a single share traded as high as $75.21.
By then, Crocs were on sale in over 13,000 store locations in the United States.
A shoe for boats had become a fashion craze. What could go wrong? The company was building as if the craze would never end.
But a craze has one problem. Sooner or later, everyone who wants one has one. And then what do you sell them?
Chapter three. The crack, and the first warning signs.
So when did it start to go wrong? The share price gave the first warning. In those same last months of the year, it fell as low as $33.75.
Why did that matter so much? Look inside the warehouse. At the end of one year, Crocs held $86.2M of inventory. A year later, it held $248.4M.
The company explained why. It had stocked up to meet the demand it expected in the first half of the next year.
That demand never came. That was the decision that broke Crocs: it built for a craze that was already ending.
The trouble was in the stores. The shops had ordered as if the craze would keep growing, and it didn't.
To see why, you need to know how a shoe brand really sells. It sells to shops first. The shops sell to you. So the brand's sales move months before yours do.
When shoppers slow down, the shops stop reordering. And the brand's sales don't just slow. They fall off a cliff.
Crocs' own annual report put it plainly. Sales were lower than many of its retailers had projected, so they cut their orders to clear their shelves.
And the shops started discounting.
Then the copies. The filing names competitors selling imitation products at substantially lower prices.
And in the same sentence, the company admits the hardest part: its products had reached a more mature stage in their life.
In plain words: the people who wanted Crocs had bought them.
And it got worse. The world economy fell into recession, and the report warned that sales could fall further in the Americas, Europe and Asia.
Then, all through 2008, every three months, the lowest price for a share sank lower than the time before.
By the end of 2008, the question was no longer how fast Crocs could grow. It was whether Crocs would still exist.
Chapter four. The crash, and how close Crocs came to the end.
How bad did it get? Sales fell to $721.6M.
Where did it show first? In the shops themselves. Crocs' sales to retailers fell 25.3% in a single year.
It sold 35.3M pairs, down from 46.9M.
Even the charms slowed. Jibbitz sales dropped to $47.2M.
Crocs wrote down $76.3M of its own shoes, styles and colours nobody wanted any more.
A write-down is what a company records when the things it owns are worth less than it paid for them. Here, that meant shoes nobody would buy at full price.
It sold them off through discount retailers, its outlet stores and warehouse sales, and gave some away.
Some of the shoes went to its own charity, Soles United.
By the end of the year, it had cut its inventory down to $143.2M.
It shut its manufacturing in Canada, where the shoe was born, and in Brazil.
It went from 5,300 employees to about 3,700.
And for the year, Crocs lost $185.1M.
A share that had traded at $75.21 now traded as low as $0.79. Less than a dollar.
A share price is the market's bet on a company's future. In those months, the market was betting Crocs had very little future at all.
Could it even pay its bank? Its main credit line was due within weeks.
And the company's auditors wrote that they had substantial doubt it could continue as a going concern.
In plain words: the people checking its books were not sure Crocs would make it through the next year.
Did it survive? It did. Barely. But sales kept falling, to $645.8M.
And then came the joke. In 2010, TIME magazine put Crocs on its list of the worst inventions.
TIME's entry noted that Crocs was already turning out heels and loafers, with ballet flats on the way. The company's chief executive told it that a little more style would reach a wider audience.
In other words, the answer to the joke was to make Crocs that didn't look like Crocs.
The craze was over. The shoe was a punchline. And the company still had one thing nobody else had.
Chapter five. The flat years, when the clog was a punchline.
So let's take stock. In a few short years, Crocs had gone from a boat shoe to 46.9M pairs a year, and then to a share worth less than a dollar.
So how do you come back from being a punchline? Slowly. Crocs climbed back. Within a few years, sales were around $1.2B, more than at the height of the craze.
In 2014, the investment firm Blackstone put $200M into the company, in return for a new class of preferred shares.
That same year, Crocs announced a plan to fix itself: fewer products, fewer small markets, less overhead, and fewer of its own stores.
By the end of that year, it had closed 104 stores.
But was it really back? Not quite. Sales stopped growing. For years, they went sideways.
And the clog was still the shoe people loved to mock.
So Crocs shrank itself. It closed stores. It ended a store reduction programme with 383 of its own shops left.
And in 2018, it stopped making shoes in its own factories, in Mexico and Italy.
From then on, other companies made its shoes, mostly in Vietnam and China.
It even moved its headquarters, from little Niwot to an office park in Broomfield, Colorado.
A smaller company. Fewer stores. The same ugly shoe. But before all that was done, the fashion world did something nobody expected.
Chapter six. The canvas, and an unlikely comeback.
Who would put a punchline on a runway? In October 2017, the luxury house Balenciaga sent Crocs down its runway in Paris, on platform soles.
Balenciaga's version went on pre-order for $850 a pair. It sold out in hours.
A shoe that had once been dumped in clearance bins was now selling, in one version, for $850.
A year later, Crocs released a clog with the rapper Post Malone. It sold out almost instantly.
Then came more. Crocs' own annual report lists partners from Justin Bieber to Balenciaga to a ranch dressing, Hidden Valley.
The joke had flipped. Wearing an ugly shoe on purpose became the point.
Why did it work this time? Because the holes Jibbitz had filled years earlier were now the business. Crocs began selling each clog as a blank canvas.
Crocs' latest annual report describes it as increased personalisation, through Jibbitz charms.
Its latest annual report calls the clog, its sandals and Jibbitz charms its key product pillars, and the Classic Clog its icon.
Here's why that matters. A charm is small, and you can add a new one any time. The shoe stays the same. What it says about you changes.
Then, in 2020, the pandemic hit, and Crocs gave away more than 860,000 pairs, many of them to frontline healthcare workers.
The clog was back on hospital floors, where Crocs at Work had once sold it.
Shoppers stuck at home bought online. In 2020, 25.9% of Crocs' sales came through its websites and online marketplaces.
So what was different from the first boom? Here is the detail that explains the comeback. Crocs raised prices on some shoes and cut its discounts.
The exact opposite of what had happened in the crash.
The next year proved it. Higher average prices alone added $265.9M to Crocs' sales.
That year, sales reached $2.31B.
And it sold 103M pairs of shoes. At the height of the original craze, it sold 46.9M.
The ugly shoe was bigger than it had ever been. So Crocs made its biggest bet yet, and this time it borrowed to make it.
So far: a craze, a crash, a decade of jokes, and a comeback built on charms and higher prices. Which brings us to the last chapter of the story so far.
Chapter seven. The second bet, and what it has cost so far.
And what do you do with a comeback that big? In February 2022, Crocs bought another shoe brand, HEYDUDE, for about $2.3B.
HEYDUDE makes light, casual shoes. Crocs said the deal would diversify the business by adding a second brand.
Most of what Crocs paid was for the name itself. On its books, the HEYDUDE trademark alone was valued at $1.57B.
It paid most of it in cash, and borrowed to do it.
HEYDUDE brought in $895.9M in its first months under Crocs.
That first year, HEYDUDE made up about 25% of Crocs' sales, but about 62% of everything the company owned, on paper.
If that sounds familiar, it should. Once again, Crocs was betting big.
Did the bet pay off? Not yet. Last year, Crocs took a $738.1M charge, mostly to cut what HEYDUDE's name and goodwill were worth on its books.
An impairment is an accounting admission. It says: this is worth less than we thought.
Of the charge, $430M came off the value of that one name.
HEYDUDE's own sales fell 13.3% last year.
Crocs now says its main goal for HEYDUDE is simply to stabilise it in the United States.
Even so, the whole company still sold $4.04B, according to its latest annual report. The Crocs brand alone brought in $3.33B.
So where are all those clogs going now? Not only to America. Almost half of Crocs brand sales, 48.6%, now come from outside the United States.
Crocs now focuses on a handful of markets: China, India, Japan, South Korea, the United States and Western Europe.
Today the company runs 514 stores of its own.
Today the company employs more than 8,010 people, most of them in its own stores.
A shoe first made in a Quebec factory is now made mostly in Vietnam and China, and sold from Shenzhen to Rotterdam.
So what really happened to Crocs? And what does it teach us about any craze?
The first time, Crocs sold a novelty. It filled every shop and every warehouse, and when the novelty wore off, it had to dump the shoes at a discount.
The second time, it sold the same shoe as a canvas. The charms changed, the collaborations changed, and the price stayed up.
The shoe never really changed. What changed was the reason to buy another pair, and then another after that.
The whole story fits in a few figures. 46.9M pairs at the peak. A share at $0.79 at the bottom. And $4.04B in sales today.
There's a lesson in that for any craze. A fad sells to everyone once. A habit sells to the same people again and again. Crocs learned the first half the hard way, and then it learned the second.
And a company's own annual report will tell you which one it is, if you read the part about discounts. Crocs said it plainly, both times.
And it shows the warning signs of any craze ending. The shops stop reordering. Discounts spread. And copies show up at lower prices.
So the best place to see whether a craze is ending isn't the adverts. It's the clearance racks, and the annual report.
So, did you own a pair the first time around, or did you only buy your first pair recently? Tell us in the comments, and tell us which charm you would pick.
Thanks for watching this story, told from the public record.
